title: Why Families Buy Gold on Dhanteras: The Legends Behind Diwali's First Day
excerpt: A healer god, a dazzled god of death, and centuries of household saving — the story of how one festival day made gold-buying a ritual that survives record prices.
body:
• Dhanteras — from dhan (wealth) and teras (the thirteenth lunar day) — opens the Diwali festival on Friday, November 6 this year, and buying gold or silver is its best-known custom.
  • Two legends anchor the tradition: Lord Dhanvantari emerging from the churning of the ocean with the nectar of immortality, and King Hima's son, saved when lamplight and piled gold dazzled Yama, the god of death.
  • Gold is tied to Goddess Lakshmi and to wealth that can be stored, gifted and passed down — which is why families buy at least a token coin even in years of high prices.
  • Modern buyers split the custom three ways: jewellery and coins, digital gold, and regulated routes such as gold ETFs and Sovereign Gold Bonds.

Ask most Indian families and they will say Dhanteras is not complete without a little gold. The festival — Dhanatrayodashi, the thirteenth lunar day of Krishna Paksha in the month of Kartik — marks the official beginning of Diwali, and it falls on Friday, November 6 this year. Understanding why millions buy gold on this one day means holding two ideas at once: it is a ritual, and it is also how Indian households have saved for centuries, as Aditya Birla Capital's explainer puts it — a blend of spiritual tradition and financial prudence.

The healer who came out of the ocean

The first legend is about health, not money. According to Hindu tradition, Lord Dhanvantari — the divine physician, an incarnation of Vishnu — emerged during the Samudra Manthan, the churning of the ocean, carrying a pot of amrit, the nectar of immortality. His appearance is the origin of Ayurveda, and Dhanteras is also observed as Dhanvantari Jayanti. Goddess Lakshmi is linked to the same churning-of-the-ocean tradition, which is how one festival day came to join wealth and health together: worship on Dhanteras is directed to Lakshmi for prosperity and to Dhanvantari for well-being.

The prince, the lamps and the gold

The second legend explains the gold directly. The son of King Hima was predicted to die by snakebite on the fourth night of his marriage. His wife kept him awake through that night, lit countless lamps, and placed gold and silver ornaments around the room. When Yama arrived in the form of a serpent, the dazzle of lamplight on precious metal stopped him at the door; by dawn he left empty-handed and the prince lived. The story is still re-enacted as Yama Deepam, the lamp lit outside the home on Dhanteras as a prayer for protection and long life — and it fixed precious metal at the centre of the festival, as MMTC-PAMP's history of the festival recounts.

Why gold, specifically

Gold and silver are considered pure and sacred metals, associated with Lakshmi; bringing them home is believed to invite her blessings for the year ahead. But the custom survived because it was also practical. Before banks and digital accounts, families held wealth as jewellery, coins and utensils — portable, divisible and inheritable. Buying on an auspicious day turned saving into ceremony. That dual character is why the purchase persists at record prices: as EquityPandit notes, many buyers purchase at least a small token — a coin, a ring, a pendant — to uphold the tradition regardless of the spot price.

The modern forms of an old custom

Today the same impulse runs through regulated channels as well as the jewellery store: digital gold, gold ETFs and Sovereign Gold Bonds all see Dhanteras demand, and the stock market holds a special Muhurat trading session on Diwali to mark an auspicious start to the market year. The World Gold Council reported that Indian gold ETFs recorded their biggest monthly inflow in September 2025, taking assets under management to $10 billion. For diaspora families, the token purchase has become the portable version of the ritual — a coin bought abroad, a first ETF unit for a child — carrying the same two ideas the legends carry: protection, and a store of value that outlasts the festival.
